this explains how Google smears the leap second

Smearing is a great solution to it. Any code which is using a wall clock for anything already knows that 1 second is not 1 second (there should be large warnings about this in any documentation dealing with wall clock time). Code is already used to wall clock time being skewed or even non-monotonic, so smearing a leap second into it shouldn't affect any code.
Wonder if the investment banks that have spent millions of dollars on technology to shave off a few milliseconds on their connection for trades will be affected much?

See also this video of Tom Scott's.

There is also a very serious proposal gaining a lot of traction to change how leap seconds work. Basically the idea is that instead of a 61 second minute, the extra second is smeared out over the course of an entire day. A clock on a computer will register 86400 one second ticks, but if someone with a stopwatch timed it independently, they'd find that each one of those computer seconds was actually 86401/86400 ~= 1.000011574 seconds each, and the day was actually 86401 seconds long. Google does this on their servers already, but AFAIK it's only Google and a few other early adopters.
